newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: North, South fight over world trade agenda.
newsitem.headline: North, South fight over world trade agenda.

text.p: Asian and African countries on Friday fiercely rejected efforts by the United States and some other Western countries to bring the issue of labour standards into the century-end agenda of the World Trade Organisation.

Their stance, and rejection by many of them of another big power bid to start WTO talks on global rules for investment, put in doubt whether a key declaration could be ready in time for the body's first ministerial meeting in Singapore next month.

Discussing a text put up by WTO Director-General Renato Ruggiero, envoys from Egypt, Malaysia, Thailand and Tanzania said their views were being brushed aside and warned this could threaten the cohesion of the fledgling trade agency.
They were backed by India and Indonesia, two of the major Asian trading nations.

"Any pressure or threats to any of the developing countries which do not agree to the inclusion of such new issues should be halted," Egypt's ambassador Munir Zahran told fellow mission chiefs at a meeting at the WTO's Geneva headquarters.
"Labour standards are not trade-related matters and this issue cannot fit into the declaration," said a Thai envoy, speaking on behalf of the Association of South-East Asian Nations (ASEAN).

The declaration, in principle to be endorsed by trade ministers from all 125 members of the two-year-old WTO, is important because it will set directions for world trade policies and negotiations to the year 2000 and beyond.
Malaysia's ambassador Siraj Haroun suggested on Friday the emerging economies were being treated like colonies with their views being "totally ignored and disregarded."

If issues they opposed were railroaded onto the WTO agenda at the December 9-13 Singapore gathering, in violation of the body's basic rule that decisions were taken by consensus, it would be "a tragedy," he declared.

The outbursts were sparked by a decision by Ruggiero, who has been seeking a middle way in weeks of discussion with WTO member countries, to include reference to labour standards, investment and competition policy in his draft text.
Many developing countries fear any discussion of these issues would inevitably lead to binding rules which could then be enforced through the WTO's dispute settlement mechanism.

They argue that -- despite Western protestations to the contrary -- the labour standards issue is a protectionist device, while the other two are aimed at enabling big Western and Japanese corporations to take over their domestic markets.

"It is going to be very hard to get a text finalised now before Singapore," said one envoy. But Ruggiero, who has set next Wednesday as the latest deadline, refused to give up. "We have several days left yet," he told reporters.

In his draft, Ruggiero proposes that the ministers declare their "commitment to the observance of core labour standards" and support for the work of the United Nations' International Labour Organisation (ILO) in this area.

The draft would also have the ministers say that the contribution the WTO could make to promoting thse standards would come through wider adherence to its open-trade rules and more trade liberalisation fostering economic growth.

U.S. officials, whose government argues that sceptical workers in the West must be shown the trading system is looking out for their interests as well as those of big companies, welcomed the draft's mention of the issue.

"But we would like to see it go much further," said one. The United States has made clear it wants a working group set up under the WTO to look closely at the issue and see how far labour standards can be made part of fair trading rules.

Canada and Japan, who are pushing for investment discussions with European Union support, are against bringing the labour issue into the WTO. The EU is in favour, but some of its members -- Germany and Britain -- are not.
